chapters.title: The Girl Who Named a World
Nine Years to the Kuiper Belt

text:
Across Pluto's horizon, in distant orbit around our Sun, what would you see on the bright western half of its icy heart? A frozen nitrogen glacier about one thousand kilometres wide — larger than Texas and Oklahoma combined — with zero craters.

On 13 and 14 July 2015, NASA's New Horizons spacecraft flew within twelve thousand five hundred kilometres of Pluto — thirty-nine times farther from the Sun than Earth at minus two hundred and thirty-two degrees Celsius — and solved that mystery: while craters up to two hundred and sixty kilometres across scar the rest of Pluto, Sputnik Planitia is an active glacier where city-sized cells of solid nitrogen circulate up and down.

How can a world one-fifth the width of Earth keep a giant nitrogen heart churning, and what secret did our only spacecraft to visit Pluto discover there?

18 February 1930. At the Lowell Observatory in Flagstaff, Arizona, American astronomer Clyde Tombaugh discovers a faint world beyond Neptune — for seventy-six years considered our solar system's ninth planet.

On 14 March 1930 in Oxford, England, eleven-year-old Venetia Burney is eating breakfast when her grandfather reads aloud that scientists have discovered a ninth planet.

Venetia suggests naming it Pluto, for the Roman god of the underworld. Her grandfather forwards the name to Lowell Observatory, and it is selected.

How small was this unknown world? With an equatorial diameter of two thousand three hundred and seventy-seven kilometres, Pluto is one-fifth the width of Earth, two-thirds the diameter of Earth's Moon, and half the width of the United States.

From an average distance of five point nine billion kilometres — thirty-nine astronomical units from the Sun — sunlight takes five point five hours to reach Pluto. At noon on Pluto, the Sun is one nine-hundredth its brightness on Earth, or three hundred times as bright as our full Moon — matching twilight near sunset on Earth.

Yet for decades, a mystery hid in Pluto's sky. Why did a secret nineteen thousand kilometres away turn Pluto into a double world?

June 1978. At the Naval Observatory in Flagstaff — six miles from Lowell Observatory — astronomers refining Pluto's orbit notice images of Pluto look elongated.

The bulge cycles back and forth over six point three nine days — Pluto's rotation period. They have discovered Charon, the largest of Pluto's five known moons, alongside Nix, Hydra, Kerberos, and Styx — each under one hundred and sixty kilometres wide.

At one thousand two hundred and fourteen kilometres across, Charon is about half the size of Pluto — the largest known satellite relative to its parent body in our solar system, often called a double planet.

Charon orbits Pluto at nineteen thousand six hundred and forty kilometres. By comparison, our Moon is twenty times farther from Earth.

One day on Pluto — tilted fifty-seven degrees so it spins backwards from east to west like Venus and Uranus — takes about one hundred and fifty-three hours, or six point four Earth days, the exact time Charon takes to complete one orbit.

In mutual tidal locking, the same surfaces of Charon and Pluto always face each other, so Charon neither rises nor sets — hovering over the same spot on Pluto's surface. Why did astronomers reclassify Pluto in the year a spacecraft launched to explore it?

If you'd like more questions like this one, subscribing really helps a small channel.

19 January 2006. NASA's four-hundred-and-seventy-eight-kilogram New Horizons launches from Cape Canaveral on an Atlas V rocket at fifty-eight thousand five hundred and thirty-six kilometres an hour — the highest launch velocity attained by a human-made object relative to Earth.

Later in 2006, after astronomers found similar worlds in the Kuiper Belt — a disc-like zone beyond Neptune from thirty to fifty astronomical units from the Sun, formed four point five billion years ago — the International Astronomical Union reclassified Pluto as a dwarf planet because other objects might cross its orbital path.

Pluto's oval, two-hundred-and-forty-eight-year orbit runs from thirty to forty-nine point three astronomical units. From 1979 to 1999, Pluto was closer to the Sun than Neptune.

On 28 February 2007, a Jupiter gravity assist boosted New Horizons by fourteen thousand kilometres an hour, shortening its voyage by three years.

At 11:49 Universal Time on 14 July 2015 — after more than nine years in flight — New Horizons flew past Pluto, gathering six point two five gigabytes of data that took over fifteen months, until 25 October 2016, to transmit across four point five light-hours at one to two kilobits per second.

Before the encounter, many expected a dead, cratered relic. Case closed? Was Pluto a frozen fossil where nothing changes?

Wrong. When the pictures came down, scientists were surprised by the paradox of how active Pluto's surface is today.

Dominating Pluto is the heart-shaped nitrogen glacier Sputnik Planitia, named for Sputnik 1, Earth's first artificial satellite — about one thousand kilometres wide, larger than Texas and Oklahoma combined, and the largest known glacier in the solar system.

While craters up to two hundred and sixty kilometres across dot other parts of Pluto, the frozen nitrogen plains of Sputnik Planitia show no craters.

Instead, the glacier is patterned with city-sized convection cells — blobs of solid nitrogen circulating up and down.

Bordering those plains are rugged mountains two to three kilometres high and troughs and valleys up to six hundred kilometres long.

When Pluto is closer to the Sun, surface ices sublimate from solid to gas, forming a thin nitrogen atmosphere that Pluto's low gravity — six per cent of Earth's — extends high in altitude. Why can towering mountains stand beside a flowing glacier between minus two hundred and twenty-six and minus two hundred and forty degrees Celsius?

Here is the biggest misconception about Pluto. On Earth, water ice is a soft glacier that melts, and rock is the solid ground beneath it.

At minus two hundred and twenty-six to minus two hundred and forty degrees Celsius — over two hundred degrees below water's zero-degree freezing point — water is essentially rock-like. Pluto's two-to-three-kilometre mountains are big blocks of water ice, sometimes coated with frozen gases like methane.

Even more remarkable, on 5 August 2026, a new analysis of New Horizons imagery led by principal investigator Alan Stern found dark features along northern Sputnik Planitia — the first evidence of recently flowing liquid on Pluto.

Because Pluto's cold temperatures and thin thirteen-microbar atmosphere make liquid nitrogen rain physically impossible, those dark features provide evidence that liquid nitrogen is rising to the surface through cracks from basal melting underneath the glacier.

And beneath its water-ice mantle, Pluto's warmer interior shows hints of an internal water-ice ocean deep inside today. What if New Horizons looked back — and where does Pluto have a captured twin?

Looking back from two hundred thousand kilometres away on 14 July 2015, New Horizons captured its farewell colour portrait of Pluto's receding crescent and blue atmospheric haze.

On 1 January 2019, six point four billion kilometres from Earth, New Horizons flew within three thousand five hundred kilometres of Arrokoth, a thirty-five-kilometre-long world and the most distant target in history.

And on 1 October 2024, speeding away at three hundred million miles per year, New Horizons passed sixty times Earth's distance from the Sun — twice as far out as Pluto was during its 2015 flyby.

Pluto showed a world one-fifth the width of Earth can hold water-ice mountains, a moon that never sets, and a nitrogen heart with zero craters.

Next in our Real Worlds series, we travel inward to Neptune's largest moon, Triton — a captured Kuiper Belt cousin of Pluto that orbits backwards and erupts active geysers on a frozen nitrogen crust at minus two hundred and thirty-five degrees Celsius.
